The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure.

1. If $\nu$ is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable real-valued functions $f$ satisfying the measurable-set integral formula in that theorem.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), if $\nu$ is a finite complex measure and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of complex $L^1(\mu)$ functions $h$ satisfying
   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

Assume AC. If $\mu$ and $\nu$ are sigma-finite positive measures on the same
measurable space and $\nu\ll\mu$, then the Radon–Nikodym class
$d\nu/d\mu$ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every
finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative
$\mu$-almost everywhere.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

derivations.claim: Put $h=\min\{f,g\}$. It is measurable and nonnegative by [F5]. Thus $\eta(A)=\int_Ah\,d\lambda$ is a measure by [F3]. Let $\theta$ be any measure with $\theta\le\rho$ and $\theta\le\sigma$. Then $\theta(E)\le\rho(E)<\infty$, so $\theta$ is finite. If $\lambda(B)=0$, then $\rho(B)=\int_Bf\,d\lambda=0$; hence $\theta(B)\le\rho(B)=0$. Therefore $\theta\ll\lambda$. It is sigma-finite because it is finite [F1]. By [A1] and [F2], choose a finite-valued nonnegative measurable density $k$ with $\theta(A)=\int_Ak\,d\lambda$ for every $A$.

For each integer $n\ge1$, set $E_n=\{k\ge f+1/n\}$. This set is measurable by [F5]. Monotonicity, additivity, and homogeneity [F4] give $$\theta(E_n)=\int_{E_n}k\,d\lambda\ge\int_{E_n}f\,d\lambda+ \frac{\lambda(E_n)}n=\rho(E_n)+\frac{\lambda(E_n)}n.$$ But $\theta(E_n)\le\rho(E_n)<\infty$, so $\lambda(E_n)=0$. Hence $$N:=\bigcup_{n\ge1}(E_n\cup G_n)$$ is $\lambda$-null, and $k\le f$ and $k\le g$, thus $k\le h$, on $E\setminus N$.

Absolute continuity gives $\theta(A)=\theta(A\setminus N)$ for every $A$, and [F6] gives $\eta(A)=\eta(A\setminus N)$. On $A\setminus N$, $k\le h$, so monotonicity [F4] yields $$\theta(A)=\int_{A\setminus N}k\,d\lambda\le \int_{A\setminus N}h\,d\lambda=\eta(A).$$ Thus every common lower measure is dominated by $\eta$.
Step 1.1 shows that $\eta$ is dominated by both $\rho$ and $\sigma$; step 3.1 shows every measure dominated by both is itself dominated by $\eta$. Therefore $\eta$ is the greatest common submeasure.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite positive
measure on $(E,\mathcal F)$, and let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be finite positive
measures absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda$. Suppose finite-valued
nonnegative measurable functions $f,g:E\to[0,\infty)$ satisfy
$$\rho(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda,\qquad \sigma(A)=\int_A g\,d\lambda\qquad(A\in\mathcal F).$$
Then
$$\eta(A):=\int_A\min\{f,g\}\,d\lambda$$
is the greatest measure dominated by both $\rho$ and $\sigma$, where
domination means inequality on every measurable set.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure.

1. If $\nu$ is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable real-valued functions $f$ satisfying the measurable-set integral formula in that theorem.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), if $\nu$ is a finite complex measure and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of complex $L^1(\mu)$ functions $h$ satisfying
   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

derivations.claim: Put $\Lambda=\lambda\otimes\lambda$. The lift $(x,y)\mapsto p(x)$ is product-measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B$ is the rectangle $p^{-1}(B)\times\mathsf X$. Each section $C_x$ is measurable: for fixed $x$, the class of all $D\subseteq\mathsf X^2$ with $D_x\in\mathcal X$ is a sigma-algebra containing every measurable rectangle, so it contains $\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$. Since $q$ and $\mathbf1_C$ are product-measurable, [F6] makes their product measurable, and [F5] makes $$H(x):=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_C(x,y)q(x,y)\,\lambda(dy)=Q(x,C_x)$$ measurable, where the equality is the given density identity for $Q(x,\cdot)$. The density identity for $\pi$ and [F10], first for simple functions and then for $H$ by [F9] and monotone convergence, give $$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}H(x)\,\pi(dx)=\int_{\mathsf X}H(x)p(x)\,\lambda(dx).$$ Substituting the expression for $H$ and applying Tonelli [F5] yields $$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}\!\int_{\mathsf X} \mathbf1_C(x,y)p(x)q(x,y)\,\lambda(dy)\lambda(dx)=\int_Cm\,d\Lambda.$$ Thus $m$ is a density of the forward probability flow with respect to $\Lambda$.

Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and define $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}(C)=\Lambda(\tau^{-1}C)$. By [F7], $\tau$ is measurable, so $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}$ is a measure. On a rectangle $A\times B$, $$\Lambda^{\mathsf T}(A\times B)=\lambda(B)\lambda(A) =\lambda(A)\lambda(B)=\Lambda(A\times B),$$ using the product-measure convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Choose increasing measurable $X_n\uparrow\mathsf X$ with $\lambda(X_n)<\infty$. The rectangles $X_n\times X_n$ increase to $\mathsf X^2$ and have equal finite measure for $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}$ and $\Lambda$. Measurable rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F3]–[F4] give $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}=\Lambda$. For every nonnegative product-measurable $u$, the identity $$\int_{\tau^{-1}C}u\,d\Lambda=\int_Cu\circ\tau\,d\Lambda$$ holds first for indicators from $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}=\Lambda$, then for simple functions by finite addition, and for all such $u$ by [F9]. Applying it to $u=m$ yields $$\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)=\int_Cm(y,x)\,d\Lambda.$$ Hence $m^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=p(y)q(y,x)$ is the reverse-flow density.

Apply [F8] to the finite probability measures $\mu,\mu^{\mathsf T}$ and the sigma-finite reference measure $\Lambda$. Their greatest common submeasure $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$ has density $h=\min\{m,m^{\mathsf T}\}$, so $$\eta(C)=\int_Ch\,d\Lambda\qquad(C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X).$$

Define $\alpha_{\rm cd}=h/m$ on $\{m>0\}$ and $\alpha_{\rm cd}=1$ on $\{m=0\}$. It takes values in $[0,1]$. For a real $c<0$, $\{\alpha_{\rm cd}>c\}=\mathsf X^2$; for $0\le c<1$, $$\{\alpha_{\rm cd}>c\}=\{m=0\}\cup \bigl(\{m>0\}\cap\{h-cm>0\}\bigr);$$ for $c\ge1$ the set is empty. Each set is measurable by [F6], so $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ is jointly measurable. By its definition, $\alpha_{\rm cd}m=h$ everywhere. For any $C$, choose nonnegative simple $s_n\uparrow\alpha_{\rm cd}\mathbf1_C$. The simple density identity [F10] gives $\int s_n\,d\mu=\int s_nm\,d\Lambda$; monotone convergence on both sides then gives $$\int_C\alpha_{\rm cd}\,d\mu=\int_C\alpha_{\rm cd}m\,d\Lambda =\int_Ch\,d\Lambda=\eta(C).$$ Thus $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ is a version of $d\eta/d\mu$.

On $\{m>0\}$, algebra gives $$\alpha_{\rm cd}=\frac{\min\{m,m^{\mathsf T}\}}m =\min\left\{1,\frac{p(y)q(y,x)}{p(x)q(x,y)}\right\}.$$ On $\{m=0\}$ its specified value is $1$, which is permissible because $\mu(\{m=0\})=\int_{\{m=0\}}m\,d\Lambda=0$. The algorithm's chosen derivative and $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ are two versions of the same Radon–Nikodym derivative, so [F11] makes them equal $\mu$-almost everywhere. This proves the common-density ratio and the forward-zero convention without asserting pointwise uniqueness on null sets.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be finite positive
measures on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal F)$. Put $\lambda=\rho+\sigma$.
Choose nonnegative measurable Radon–Nikodym density representatives
$f=d\rho/d\lambda$ and $g=d\sigma/d\lambda$, modified on a $\lambda$-null set
so that $f+g=1$ everywhere. Then
$$\eta(A):=\int_A\min\{f,g\}\,d\lambda\qquad(A\in\mathcal F)$$
is the greatest measure dominated by both $\rho$ and $\sigma$. The measurable
function
$$a:=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g/f\},&f>0,\\1,&f=0\end{cases}$$
takes values in $[0,1]$ and is a version of $d\eta/d\rho$. Here $\eta\le\rho$
means $\eta(A)\le\rho(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal F$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, $P$ a probability kernel
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on it, and $\pi$ a probability
measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it. If $P$ is reversible with
respect to $\pi$ in the sense of
[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]], then $\pi$ is
invariant for $P$: for every $A\in\mathcal X$,

$$\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A).$$

derivations.claim: The acceptance function satisfies $0\le\alpha\le1$. For each $x$, $0\le a(x):=\int\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)\le1$ because $Q(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure. The function $a$ is measurable by [F5], so $r(x)=1-a(x)$ is measurable and takes values in $[0,1]$.

For fixed $x$, the accepted term $A\mapsto\int\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)$ is a measure by [F9], since the section $y\mapsto\alpha(x,y)$ is measurable by [F8]. The rejection term $A\mapsto r(x)\mathbf1_A(x)$ is a measure: for disjoint sets at most one can contain $x$. Their sum is a measure by [F10], and its total mass is $a(x)+r(x)=1$. For each fixed $A$, the accepted term is measurable in $x$ by [F5], and the rejection term is measurable since $r$ and $\mathbf1_A$ are measurable. Thus [F2] applies pointwise and $P$ is a probability kernel.

Define $\delta(x)=(x,x)$. For every measurable rectangle $A\times B$, $\delta^{-1}(A\times B)=A\cap B\in\mathcal X$. Since these rectangles generate $\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ by [F7], $\delta$ is measurable. By [F9], $\zeta(D):=\int_D r\,d\pi$ is a measure on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$; it is finite because $0\le r\le1$ and $\pi(\mathsf X)=1$. Define $R(C):=\zeta(\delta^{-1}C)=\int\mathbf1_C(x,x)r(x)\,\pi(dx)$. It vanishes at the empty set, and preimages of disjoint sets under $\delta$ are disjoint; countable additivity of $\zeta$ therefore makes $R$ a finite measure on the product sigma-algebra.

Step 1.2 has established that $P$ is a probability kernel, so [F3] now supplies the joint measure $J_P$. Applying the same joint-law result to the input kernel $Q$ gives the proposal flow $\mu$ and its iterated-integral identity. Thus, for every product-measurable $C$, $$J_P(C)=\int\!\int\mathbf1_C(x,y)\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)\,\pi(dx)+R(C)=\int_C\alpha\,d\mu+R(C)=\eta(C)+R(C),$$ where the last equality uses $\alpha\,\mu=\eta$ from [F4].

The coordinate swap $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ is measurable by [F7] and is an involution. Since $\eta$ is the greatest measure dominated by both $\mu$ and $\mu^{\mathsf T}$, its transpose $\eta^{\mathsf T}$ is also dominated by both: for every $C$, $\eta^{\mathsf T}(C)=\eta(\tau^{-1}C)\le\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)$ and $\eta^{\mathsf T}(C)\le\mu(C)$. Maximality gives $\eta^{\mathsf T}\le\eta$; transposing this inequality and using $\tau^2=\mathrm{id}$ gives $\eta\le\eta^{\mathsf T}$. Hence $\eta^{\mathsf T}=\eta$.

Since $\tau\circ\delta=\delta$, step 2.1 gives $R(C)=R(\tau^{-1}C)$ for every product-measurable $C$. Step 3.1 gives the same symmetry for $\eta$, so the decomposition in step 2.2 yields $J_P(C)=J_P(\tau^{-1}C)$ for every $C$. Thus the joint flow is symmetric, so $P$ is reversible by [F11].

Steps 1.2 and 3.2 prove that $P$ is a probability kernel reversible with respect to $\pi$. The general-state result [F12] applies on this measurable space and gives $\int P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal X$. Thus $\pi$ is invariant in the sense of [F6].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be standard Borel
([[def-standard-borel-space]]) and let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite positive
measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on it. Let the
target probability have a finite-valued nonnegative measurable density
$p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$, and suppose the proposal kernel has a finite-valued
nonnegative jointly measurable density $q:\mathsf X\times\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$,
so $\pi(A)=\int_Ap\,d\lambda$ and
$Q(x,A)=\int_Aq(x,y)\,d\lambda(y)$ for every $x$ and $A$. Let
$\mu(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)Q(x,dy)$ be the forward proposal flow and let
$\mu^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose. Put
$$m(x,y)=p(x)q(x,y),\qquad m^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=p(y)q(y,x).$$
There is a jointly measurable version $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ of
$d(\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T})/d\mu$ given by
$$\alpha_{\rm cd}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\left\{1,\dfrac{p(y)q(y,x)}{p(x)q(x,y)}\right\},&m(x,y)>0,\\1,&m(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
The version chosen by [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] agrees with this
common-density version $\mu$-almost everywhere; values on a forward-flow null
set do not alter the accepted flow.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be standard Borel
([[def-standard-borel-space]]) and let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite positive
measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on it. Let the
target probability have a finite-valued nonnegative measurable density
$p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$, and suppose the proposal kernel has a finite-valued
nonnegative jointly measurable density $q:\mathsf X\times\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$,
so $\pi(A)=\int_Ap\,d\lambda$ and
$Q(x,A)=\int_Aq(x,y)\,d\lambda(y)$ for every $x$ and $A$. Let
$\mu(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)Q(x,dy)$ be the forward proposal flow and let
$\mu^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose. Put
$$m(x,y)=p(x)q(x,y),\qquad m^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=p(y)q(y,x).$$
There is a jointly measurable version $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ of
$d(\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T})/d\mu$ given by
$$\alpha_{\rm cd}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\left\{1,\dfrac{p(y)q(y,x)}{p(x)q(x,y)}\right\},&m(x,y)>0,\\1,&m(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
The version chosen by [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] agrees with this
common-density version $\mu$-almost everywhere; values on a forward-flow null
set do not alter the accepted flow.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.
